{{short description|Solution of Einstein field equations}}
{{general relativity sidebar|solutions}}
The '''Kerr–Newman metric''' describes the [[spacetime|spacetime geometry]] around a mass that is electrically charged and rotating. It is a [[vacuum solution]] that generalizes the [[Kerr metric]] (which describes an uncharged, rotating mass) by additionally taking into account the energy of an [[electromagnetic field]], making it the most general [[asymptotically flat]] and [[stationary spacetime|stationary solution]] of the [[Einstein's field equation#Einstein–Maxwell equations|Einstein–Maxwell equations]] in [[general relativity]]. As an [[electrovacuum solution]], it only includes those charges associated with the magnetic field; it does not include any free electric charges. 

The Kerr–Newman metric is primarily of theoretical interest. Astronomical objects have axes for rotation and for magnetic fields, but the metric is only valid for co-aligned axes.
The model lacks description of infalling [[baryonic matter]], light ([[null dust solution|null dusts]]) or [[dark matter]], and thus provides an incomplete description of [[stellar black hole|stellar mass black holes]] and [[active galactic nuclei]]. The solution however is of mathematical interest and provides a fairly simple cornerstone for further exploration.

== History ==
In December of 1963, [[Roy Kerr]] and [[Alfred Schild]] found the Kerr–Schild metrics that gave all [[Einstein manifold|Einstein spaces]] that are exact linear perturbations of [[Minkowski space]]. In early 1964, Kerr looked for all Einstein–Maxwell spaces with this same property. By February of 1964, the special case where the Kerr–Schild spaces were charged (including the Kerr–Newman solution) was known but the general case where the special directions were not geodesics of the underlying Minkowski space proved very difficult. The problem was given to George Debney to try to solve but was given up by March 1964. About this time Ezra T. Newman found the solution for charged Kerr by guesswork.
In 1965, [[Ezra T. Newman|Ezra "Ted" Newman]] found the axisymmetric solution of Einstein's field equation for a black hole which is both rotating and electrically charged.<ref name=Newman-1965>{{cite journal |last1=Newman |first1=Ezra |last2=Janis |first2=Allen |title=Note on the Kerr Spinning-Particle Metric |journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Physics]] |volume=6 |issue=6 |pages=915–917 |date=1965 |doi=10.1063/1.1704350 |bibcode = 1965JMP.....6..915N }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Newman |first1=Ezra |last2=Couch |first2=E. |last3=Chinnapared |first3=K. |last4=Exton |first4=A. |last5=Prakash |first5=A. |last6=Torrence |first6=R. |title=Metric of a Rotating, Charged Mass |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=6 |issue=6 |pages=918–919 |date=1965 |doi=10.1063/1.1704351 |bibcode = 1965JMP.....6..918N }}</ref> This formula for the [[metric tensor]] is called the Kerr–Newman metric. It is a generalisation of the [[Kerr metric]] for an uncharged spinning point-mass, which had been discovered by Roy Kerr two years earlier.<ref name="kerr_1963">{{cite journal | last = Kerr | first = RP | author-link = Roy Kerr | date = 1963 | title = Gravitational field of a spinning mass as an example of algebraically special metrics | journal = Physical Review Letters | volume = 11 | issue = 5 | pages = 237–238 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.11.237 | bibcode=1963PhRvL..11..237K }}</ref>

== Overview of the solution ==
[[File:Spinning_and_chargend_black_hole_with_accretion_disk.jpg|220px|thumb|[[Ray tracing (physics)|Ray traced]] shadow of a spinning and charged black hole with an accretion disk and parameters {{nowrap|1=''a''/''M'' = 0.95}}, {{nowrap|1=''Q''/''M'' = 0.3}}. The left side of the black hole is rotating towards the observer, the tilt of the rotation axis relative to the observer is 45°.]]
Newman's result represents the simplest [[stationary spacetime|stationary]], [[axial symmetry|axisymmetric]], asymptotically flat solution of [[Einstein's equations]] in the presence of an [[electromagnetic field]] in four dimensions. It is sometimes referred to as an "electrovacuum" solution of Einstein's equations.

The solution contains a singularity in the shape of a ring.
The multipole structure of the solution suggests that the solution represents the field of a ring of charge rotating about its axis of symmetry. Similarly the Kerr solution represents the field of a ring of mass. However, for this simple view to be mathematically correct, charge (or mass in the Kerr case) needs to be distributed around the singular ring of the solution to break the multivalued behavior.<ref name=Newman-1965/>

Any Kerr–Newman source has its rotation axis aligned with its magnetic axis.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Punsly |first=Brian |title=High-energy gamma-ray emission from galactic Kerr–Newman black holes. I. The central engine |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=10 May 1998 |volume=498 |issue=2 |doi=10.1086/305561 |page=646 |bibcode=1998ApJ...498..640P |quote=All Kerr–Newman black holes have their rotation axis and magnetic axis aligned; they cannot pulse. |doi-access=free }}</ref> Thus, a Kerr–Newman source is different from commonly observed astronomical bodies, for which there is a substantial angle between the rotation axis and the [[magnetic moment]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Lang |first=Kenneth |year=2003  |title=The Cambridge Guide to the Solar System |page=[https://archive.org/details/cambridgeguideto0000lang/page/96 96] |publisher=Cambridge University Press |url=https://archive.org/details/cambridgeguideto0000lang |url-access=registration |quote=magnetic dipole moment and axis and the sun. |via=Internet Archive|isbn=978-0-521-81306-8 }}</ref> Specifically, neither the [[Sun]], nor any of the [[planet]]s in the [[Solar System]] has its magnetic field dipole aligned with its spin axis. Thus, while the Kerr solution describes the gravitational field of the Sun and planets, the magnetic fields necessarily arise by a different process.

== Limiting cases ==
The Kerr–Newman metric can be seen to reduce to other [[exact solutions in general relativity]] in limiting cases. It reduces to<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Reinhard Meinel |first=Reinhard |last=Meinel |chapter=A Physical Derivation of the Kerr–Newman Black Hole Solution |editor=Nicolini P. |editor2=Kaminski M. |editor3=Mureika J. |editor4=Bleicher M. |title=1st Karl Schwarzschild Meeting on Gravitational Physics |series=Springer Proceedings in Physics |volume=170 |pages=53–61 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-20046-0_6 |isbn=978-3-319-20045-3 |date=29 October 2015 |arxiv=1310.0640 |s2cid=119200468 }}</ref>{{rp|61}}
* the [[Kerr metric]] as the charge ''Q'' goes to zero;
* the [[Reissner–Nordström metric]] as the angular momentum ''J'' (or {{nowrap|1=''a'' = ''J''/''M''}}) goes to zero;
* the [[Schwarzschild metric]] as both the charge ''Q'' and the angular momentum ''J'' (or ''a'') are taken to zero; and
* [[Minkowski space]] if the mass ''M'', the charge ''Q'', and the rotational parameter ''a'' are all zero.

The four related solutions may be summarized by the following table:
: {| class="wikitable"
|-
 !
 ! Non-rotating (''J'' = 0)
 ! Rotating (any ''J'')
|-
 ! Uncharged (''Q'' = 0)
 | [[Schwarzschild metric|Schwarzschild]]
 | [[Kerr metric| Kerr]]
|-
 ! Charged (any ''Q'')
 | [[Reissner–Nordström metric|Reissner–Nordström]]
 | Kerr–Newman
|-
|}

where ''Q'' is the body's [[electric charge]] and ''J'' is its spin [[angular momentum]].

Taking the gravitational constant {{mvar|G}} to be zero in the Kerr–Newman solution gives an electromagnetic field from a rotating charged disk with a boundary in a [[Minkowski space]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lynden-Bell |first=D. |date=November 29, 2004 |title=Electromagnetic magic: The relativistically rotating disk |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.70.105017 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=70 |issue=10 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.70.105017 |issn=1550-7998|arxiv=gr-qc/0410109 }}</ref><ref name=Newman-2014/> The Kerr–Newman solution itself is a special case of more general exact solutions of the Einstein–Maxwell equations. The more general solutions include a [[cosmological constant]], a [[Taub–NUT space|Newman, Unti, Tamburino (NUT)]] parameter, and a [[Magnetic monopole|magnetic charge]].<ref name="Exact" />{{rp|324}}

== Metric field ==
The Kerr–Newman metric describes the geometry of [[spacetime]] for a rotating charged black hole with mass ''M'', charge ''Q'' and angular momentum ''J''. The formula for this metric depends upon what coordinates or [[coordinate conditions]] are selected. Two forms are given below: Boyer–Lindquist coordinates, and Kerr–Schild coordinates. The gravitational metric alone is not sufficient to determine a solution to the Einstein field equations; the electromagnetic stress tensor must be given as well. Both are provided in each section.

== Boyer–Lindquist coordinates ==
{{main|Boyer–Lindquist coordinates}}
One way to express this metric is by writing down its [[line element]] in a particular set of [[Spherical coordinate system|spherical coordinates]],<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hájíček |first1=P. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1vEe-8ktTJsC&pg=PA243 |title=An introduction to the relativistic theory of gravitation |last2=Meyer |first2=Frank |last3=Metzger |first3=Jan |date=2008 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-78658-0 |series=Lecture notes in physics |location=Berlin |page=243 |oclc=221218012 }}</ref> also called [[Boyer–Lindquist coordinates]]:
: <math>c^{2} d\tau^{2} = 
-\left(\frac{dr^2}{\Delta} + d\theta^2 \right) \rho^2 + \left(c \, dt - a \sin^2 \theta \, d\phi \right)^2 \frac{\Delta}{\rho^2} - \left(\left(r^2 + a^2 \right) d\phi - a c\, dt \right)^2 \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{\rho^2},</math>
where {{nowrap|(''r'', ''θ'', ''ϕ'')}} are standard [[spherical coordinate system|spherical coordinates]], and the length scales:
: <math>a = \frac{J}{Mc}\,,</math>
: <math>\rho^{2}=r^2+a^2\cos^2\theta\,,</math>
: <math>\Delta=r^2-r_\text{s}r+a^2+r_Q^2\,,</math>
have been introduced for brevity. Here ''r''<sub>s</sub> is the [[Schwarzschild radius]] of the massive body, which is related to its total mass-equivalent ''M'' by
: <math>r_\text{s} = \frac{2GM}{c^{2}},</math>
where ''G'' is the [[gravitational constant]], and ''r''<sub>''Q''</sub> is a length scale corresponding to the [[electric charge]] ''Q'' of the mass
: <math>r_{Q}^{2} = \frac{Q^{2}G}{4\pi\epsilon_{0} c^{4}},</math>
where ''ε''<sub>0</sub> is the [[vacuum permittivity]].

=== Electromagnetic field tensor in Boyer–Lindquist form ===
The electromagnetic potential in Boyer–Lindquist coordinates is<ref name=Carter-1968>{{cite journal |last=Carter |first=Brandon |date=1968-10-25 |title=Global Structure of the Kerr Family of Gravitational Fields |url=https://luth.obspm.fr/~luthier/carter/trav/Carter68.pdf#page=3 |journal=Physical Review |volume=174 |issue=5 |pages=1559–1571 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.174.1559 |bibcode=1968PhRv..174.1559C }}</ref><ref name="luongo">{{cite journal |arxiv=1407.1530|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.90.084032|title=Characterizing repulsive gravity with curvature eigenvalues|journal=Physical Review D|volume=90|issue=8|article-number=084032|year=2014|last1=Luongo|first1=Orlando|last2=Quevedo|first2=Hernando|bibcode=2014PhRvD..90h4032L|s2cid=118457584}}</ref>
: <math>A_{\mu}=\left( \frac{r \ r_Q }{\rho^2},0,0,-\frac{\ a \ r \ r_Q  \sin ^2 \theta }{\rho^2 } \right) </math>
while the Maxwell tensor is defined by
: <math>F_{\mu\nu} = \frac{\partial A_\nu}{\partial x^{\mu}} - \frac{\partial A_\mu}{\partial x^{\nu}} \ \to \ F^{\mu\nu}=g^{\mu\sigma} \ g^{\nu\kappa} \ F_{\sigma \kappa}</math>

In combination with the [[Christoffel symbols]] the second order [[#Equations of motion|equations of motion]] can be derived with
: <math>{{\ddot x^i = - \Gamma^i_{j k} \ {\dot x^j} \ {\dot x^k} + q \ {F^{i k}} \ {\dot x^j}} \ {g_{j k}}},</math>
where <math>q</math> is the charge-to-mass ratio of the test particle.

== Kerr–Schild coordinates ==
The Kerr–Newman metric can be expressed in the [[Kerr–Schild perturbations|Kerr–Schild]] form, using a particular set of [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]], proposed by [[Roy Patrick Kerr|Kerr]] and [[Alfred Schild|Schild]] in 1965. The metric is as follows.<ref name="Debney">{{cite journal |doi = 10.1063/1.1664769 |title = Solutions of the Einstein and Einstein–Maxwell Equations |journal = Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume = 10 |issue = 10 |pages = 1842–1854 |year = 1969 |last1 = Debney |first1 = G. C. |last2 = Kerr |first2 = R. P. |last3 = Schild |first3 = A. |bibcode = 1969JMP....10.1842D }} See equations (7.10), (7.11) and (7.14).</ref><ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=gr-qc/9312028 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/11/6/010 |title=Distributional energy–momentum tensor of the Kerr–Newman spacetime family |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=1 1|issue=6 |pages=1453–1461 |year=1994 |last1=Balasin |first1=Herbert |last2=Nachbagauer |first2=Herbert |bibcode=1994CQGra..11.1453B |s2cid=6041750 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Samuel Berman |first=Marcelo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DGwYf8cOCq4C&pg=PA149 |title=Trends in black hole research |date=2006 |publisher=Nova Science Publishers |isbn=978-1-59454-475-0 |editor-last=Kreitler |editor-first=Paul V. |location=New York |page=149 |oclc=ocm60671837 |display-authors=etal }}</ref>
: <math>g_{\mu \nu} = \eta_{\mu \nu} + fk_{\mu}k_{\nu} \!</math>
: <math>f = \frac{Gr^2}{r^4 + a^2z^2}\left[2Mr - Q^2 \right]</math>
: <math>\mathbf{k} = ( k_{x} ,k_{y} ,k_{z} ) = \left( \frac{rx+ay}{r^2 + a^2} , \frac{ry-ax}{r^2 + a^2}, \frac{z}{r} \right) </math>
: <math>k_{0} = 1. \!</math>

Here, '''k''' is a [[unit vector]].  Here ''M'' is the constant mass of the spinning object, ''Q'' is the constant charge of the spinning object, ''η'' is the [[Minkowski space#Standard basis|Minkowski metric]], and ''a''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''J''/''M'' is a constant rotational parameter of the spinning object.  It is understood that the vector <math>\vec{a}</math> is directed along the positive z-axis, i.e. <math>\vec{a} = a \hat{z}</math>.  The quantity ''r'' is not the radius, but rather is implicitly defined by the relation
: <math>1 = \frac{x^2+y^2}{r^2 + a^2} + \frac{z^2}{r^2}.</math>

The quantity ''r'' becomes the usual radius ''R''
: <math>r \to R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}</math>
when the rotational parameter ''a'' approaches zero.  In this form of solution, units are selected so that the speed of light is unity ({{nowrap|1=''c'' = 1}}).  In order to provide a complete solution of the [[Einstein's field equation#Einstein–Maxwell equations|Einstein–Maxwell equations]], the Kerr–Newman solution not only includes a formula for the metric tensor, but also a formula for the electromagnetic potential:<ref name="Debney" /><ref>{{cite book |title=Beyond the quantum: proceedings of the Lorentz Workshop "Beyond the Quantum", Lorentz Center Leiden, The Netherlands, 29 May – 2 June 2006 |date=2007 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-277-117-9 |editor-last=Nieuwenhuizen |editor-first=Theo M. |location=New Jersey NJ |page=321 |quote=The formula for the vector potential of Burinskii differs from that of Debney et al. merely by a gradient which does not affect the fields. |editor-last2=Philipp |editor-first2=Walter |editor-last3=Špička |editor-first3=Václav |editor-last4=Mehmani |editor-first4=Bahar |editor-last5=Aghdami |editor-first5=Maryam J. |editor-last6=Khrennikov |editor-first6=Andrei }}</ref>
: <math>A_{\mu} = \frac{Qr^3}{r^4 + a^2z^2}k_{\mu}</math>

At large distances from the source ({{nowrap|''R'' ≫ ''a''}}), these equations reduce to the [[Reissner–Nordström metric]] with:
: <math>A_{\mu} = \frac{Q}{R}k_{\mu}</math>

In the Kerr–Schild form of the Kerr–Newman metric, the determinant of the metric tensor is everywhere equal to negative one, even near the source.<ref name="Exact">{{cite book |last1=Stephani |first1=Hans |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SiWXP8FjTFEC |title=Exact Solutions of Einstein's Field Equations |last2=Kramer |first2=Dietrich |last3=MacCallum |first3=Malcolm |last4=Hoenselaers |first4=Cornelius |last5=Herlt |first5=Eduard |date=2009-09-24 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-43502-4 |page=485 |language=en}} See page 485 regarding determinant of metric tensor. See page 325 regarding generalizations.</ref>

=== Electromagnetic fields in Kerr–Schild form ===
The electric and magnetic fields can be obtained in the usual way by differentiating the four-potential to obtain the [[Electromagnetic tensor|electromagnetic field strength tensor]]. It will be convenient to switch over to three-dimensional vector notation.
: <math>A_{\mu} = \left(-\phi, A_x, A_y, A_z \right) \,</math>

The static electric and magnetic fields are derived from the vector potential and the scalar potential like this:
: <math>\vec{E} = - \vec{\nabla} \phi \,</math>
: <math>\vec{B} = \vec{\nabla} \times \vec{A} \,</math>
Using the Kerr–Newman formula for the four-potential in the Kerr–Schild form, in the limit of the mass going to zero, yields the following concise complex formula for the fields:<ref>Gair, Jonathan. [http://www.ast.cam.ac.uk/~jgair/research/kerrnewman.html "Boundstates in a Massless Kerr–Newman Potential"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110926233054/http://www.ast.cam.ac.uk/~jgair/research/kerrnewman.html |date=2011-09-26 }}</ref>
: <math>\vec{E} + i\vec{B} = -\vec{\nabla}\Omega\,</math>
: <math>\Omega = \frac{Q}{\sqrt{(\vec{R}-i\vec{a})^2}} \,</math>

The quantity omega (Ω) in this last equation is similar to the [[Electric potential#Electric potential due to a point charge|Coulomb potential]], except that the radius vector is shifted by an imaginary amount.  This complex potential was discussed as early as the nineteenth century, by the French mathematician [[Paul Émile Appell]].<ref>Appell, Math. Ann. xxx (1887) pp. 155–156.  Discussed by [[E. T. Whittaker|Whittaker, Edmund]] and [[G. N. Watson|Watson, George.]]  ''[[A Course of Modern Analysis]]'', p. 400 (Cambridge University Press 1927).</ref>

== Irreducible mass ==
The total mass-equivalent ''M'', which contains the [[Electric potential energy|electric field-energy]] and the [[rotational energy]], and the irreducible mass ''M''<sub>irr</sub> are related by<ref>[[Thibault Damour]]: [http://lapth.cnrs.fr/pg-nomin/chardon/IRAP_PhD/BlackHolesNice2012.pdf#page=11 Black Holes: Energetics and Thermodynamics], p. 11</ref><ref>Eq. 57 in {{cite journal |arxiv=1310.7126 |article-number=2887|doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-014-2887-2 |doi-access=free|title=Black hole interior mass formula |journal=The European Physical Journal C |volume=74 |issue=5 |year=2014 |last1=Pradhan |first1=Parthapratim |bibcode=2014EPJC...74.2887P |s2cid=46448376 }}</ref>
: <math>
M_{\rm irr} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 M^2-r^2_Q c^4/G^2+2 M \sqrt{M^2-(r^2_Q +a^2) c^4/G^2}}
</math>
which can be solved to obtain
: <math>
M = \frac{4 M_{\rm irr}^2+r^2_Q c^4/G^2}{2\sqrt{4 M_{\rm irr}^2- a^2 c^4/G^2}}
</math>

In order to electrically charge and/or spin a neutral and static body, energy has to be applied to the system. Due to the [[mass–energy equivalence]], this energy also has a mass-equivalent; therefore ''M'' is always higher than ''M''<sub>irr</sub>. If for example the rotational energy of a black hole is extracted via the [[Penrose process]]es,<ref name="mtw">{{cite book |last1=Misner |first1=Charles W. |author-link=Charles W. Misner |url=https://fma.if.usp.br/~mlima/teaching/PGF5292_2021/Misner_Gravitation.pdf |title=Gravitation |last2=Thorne |first2=Kip S. |author-link2=Kip Thorne |last3=Wheeler |first3=John Archibald |author-link3=John Archibald Wheeler |last4=Kaiser |first4=David |date=2017 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-17779-3 |location=Princeton, N.J |page=877, 908 |oclc=on1006427790 }}</ref><ref name="bhat">{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/BF02715080 |title=Energetics of the Kerr–Newman black hole by the penrose process |journal=Journal of Astrophysics and Astronomy |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=85–100 |year=1985 |last1=Bhat |first1=Manjiri |last2=Dhurandhar |first2=Sanjeev |last3=Dadhich |first3=Naresh |bibcode=1985JApA....6...85B |s2cid=53513572 }}</ref> the remaining mass–energy will always stay greater than or equal to ''M''<sub>irr</sub>.

== Important surfaces ==
[[File:Kerr-Flaechen_thumbnail.gif|220px|thumb|right|link=File:Kerr-surfaces.png|Event horizons and ergospheres of a charged and spinning black hole in pseudospherical {{nowrap|(''r'', ''θ'', ''φ'')}} and cartesian {{nowrap|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} coordinates.]]
Setting <math>1 / g_{rr}</math> to 0 and solving for <math>r</math> gives the inner and outer [[event horizon]], which is located at the Boyer–Lindquist coordinate
: <math>r_{\text{H}}^{\pm} = \frac{r_{\rm s}}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{r_{\rm s}^2}{4} - a^2 - r_Q^2}.</math>
Repeating this step with <math>g_{tt}</math> gives the inner and outer [[ergosurface]]
: <math>r_{\text{E}}^{\pm} = \frac{r_{\rm s}}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{r_{\rm s}^2}{4} - a^2 \cos^2\theta - r_Q^2}.</math>

The region between the event horizon and the ergosurface is called the [[ergosphere]]. Within the ergosphere all local light cones are tilted in the direction of rotation.<ref name=Newman-2014/>{{rp|18}} 

[[File:Kerr-Newman-Orbit-1-thumbnail.gif|thumb|right|220px|link=File:Kerr-Newman-Orbit-1.gif|Test particle in orbit around a spinning and charged black hole (''a''/''M''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.9, ''Q''/''M''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.4)]]

== Equations of motion ==
For brevity, we further use [[nondimensionalization|nondimensionalized quantities]] normalized against  <math>G</math>, <math>M</math>, <math>c</math> and <math>4\pi\epsilon_0</math>, where <math>a</math> reduces to <math>Jc/G/M^2</math> and <math>Q</math> to <math display="inline">Q/(M\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0G})</math>, and the equations of motion for a test particle of charge <math>q</math> become<ref name="cebeci">{{cite web |first=Hakan |last=Cebeci |display-authors=etal |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/288890529 |title=Motion of the charged test particles in Kerr–Newman–Taub–NUT spacetime and analytical solutions}}</ref><ref name="hackman">{{cite journal |first1=Eva |last1=Hackmann |first2=Hongxiao |last2=Xu |title=Charged particle motion in Kerr–Newmann space–times |journal=Physical Review D |volume=87 |issue=12 |page=4|arxiv=1304.2142 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.87.124030 |year=2013 |bibcode=2013PhRvD..87l4030H |s2cid=118576540 }}</ref>
: <math>\dot t \Delta  \rho^2 = \csc ^2 \theta \ ({L_z} (a \ \Delta  \sin ^2 \theta -a \ (a^2+r^2) \sin ^2 \theta )-q \ Q \ r \ (a^2+r^2) \sin ^2 \theta +E  ((a^2+r^2)^2 \sin ^2 \theta -a^2 \Delta  \sin ^4  \theta ))</math>
: <math>\dot r \rho^2= \pm \left(((r^2+a^2) \ E - a \ L_z - q \ Q \ r)^2-\Delta \ (C+r^2)\right)^{1/2}</math>
: <math>\dot \theta \rho^2 = \pm \left(C-(a \cos \theta)^2-(a \ \sin^2 \theta \ E-L_z)^2/\sin^2 \theta\right)^{1/2}</math>
: <math>\dot \phi \rho^2 \ \Delta \ \sin^2\theta= E \ (a \ \sin^2 \theta \ (r^2+a^2)-a \ \sin^2 \theta \ \Delta)+L_z \ (\Delta-a^2 \ \sin^2 \theta)-q \ Q \ r \ a \ \sin^2 \theta</math>
with <math>E</math> for the total energy and <math>L_z</math> for the axial angular momentum. <math>C</math> is the [[Carter constant]]:
: <math>C = p_{\theta}^{2} + \cos^{2}\theta \left( a^{2}(\mu^2 - E^{2}) + \frac{L_z^2}{ \sin^2\theta}\right) = a^2 \ (\mu^2-E^2) \ \sin^2 \delta + L_z^2 \ \tan^2 \delta = {\rm const},</math>
where <math>p_{\theta} = \dot \theta \ \rho^2</math> is the poloidial component of the test particle's angular momentum, and <math>\delta</math> the orbital inclination angle.
: <math>L_z = p_{\phi}=-g_{\phi \phi} {\dot{\phi}}-g_{t \phi} {\dot{t}} - q \ A_{\phi} = \frac{v^{\phi} \ \bar R}{\sqrt{1-\mu^2 v^2}}+\frac{(1-\mu^2 v^2) \ a \ r \ \mho \ q \ \sin ^2 \theta }{\Sigma } = {\rm const.}</math>
and
: <math>E = -p_t =g_{tt} {\dot{t}}+g_{t \phi} {\dot{\phi}} + q \ A_{t} = \sqrt{\frac{\Delta \ \rho^2}{(1-\mu^2 v^2) \ \chi}} + \Omega \ L_z +\frac{\mho \ q \ r }{\Sigma} = {\rm const.}</math>
with <math> \mu^2=0 </math> and <math> \mu^2=1 </math> for particles are also conserved quantities.
: <math>\Omega = -\frac{g_{t\phi}}{g_{\phi\phi}} = \frac{a \left(2 r-Q^2\right)}{\chi }</math>
is the frame dragging induced angular velocity. The shorthand term <math>\chi</math> is defined by
: <math>\chi = \left(a ^2+r^2\right)^2-a ^2 \ \sin ^2 \theta  \ \Delta.</math>

The relation between the coordinate derivatives <math>\dot r, \ \dot \theta, \ \dot \phi</math> and the local 3-velocity <math>v</math> is
: <math>v^{r} = \dot r \ \sqrt{\frac{\rho^2 \ (1-\mu^2 v^2)}{\Delta}}</math>
for the radial,
: <math>v^{\theta} = \dot \theta \ \sqrt{\rho^2 \ (1-\mu^2 v^2) }</math>
for the poloidial,
: <math>v^{\phi} = \sqrt{1-\mu^2 v^2} \left(L_z \ \Sigma - a \ q \ Q \ r \left( 1-\mu^2 v^2 \right) \sin^2 \theta \right)\cdot(\bar{R} \ \Sigma )^{-1}</math>
for the axial and
: <math>v =  \frac{\sqrt{\dot t^2-\varsigma^2}}{\dot t} = \sqrt{\frac{\chi \ (E-L_z \ \Omega )^2 -\Delta \ \rho^2}{\chi \ (E-L_z \ \Omega )^2}}</math>
for the total local velocity, where
: <math>\bar R = \sqrt{-g_{\phi \phi}} = \sqrt{\frac{\chi}{\rho^2}} \ \sin \theta</math>
is the axial radius of gyration (local circumference divided by 2π), and
: <math>\varsigma = \sqrt{g^{t t}}  = \frac{\chi }{\Delta \ \rho^2}</math>
the gravitational time dilation component. The local radial escape velocity for a neutral particle is therefore
: <math>v_{\rm esc}=\frac{\sqrt{\varsigma^2-1}}{\varsigma} .</math>

== Extremal solutions and naked singularity ==
For the set of parameters <math>M^2 - (J/M)^2 - Q^2 = 0</math> the solution is called "extremal"; in the super-extremal regime, <math>M^2 - (J/M)^2 - Q^2 < 0</math>, there is no event horizon and the interior singularity is observable as a [[naked singularity]]. That is, 
the Kerr–Newman metric defines a black hole with an event horizon only when the combined charge and angular momentum are sufficiently small compared to the mass.<ref name=Newman-2014/>

An electron's rotational parameter ''a'' and charge length scale ''r''<sub>''Q''</sub> both far exceed its Schwarzschild radius ''r''<sub>s</sub>, which implies that there is no event horizon, so a "black hole electron" would necessarily be a [[naked singularity|naked spinning ring singularity]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Burinskii |first=Alexander |title=The Dirac–Kerr electron |journal= Gravitation and Cosmology|volume=14 |pages=109–122 |year=2008|arxiv=hep-th/0507109 |doi=10.1134/S0202289308020011 |s2cid=119084073 }}</ref> Such a metric has several seemingly unphysical properties, such as the ring's violation of the [[cosmic censorship hypothesis]] and appearance of causality-violating [[closed timelike curve]]s in the immediate vicinity of the ring.<ref name=Carter-1968/>

== Dirac–Kerr–Newman electron model ==
In an analysis of the Kerr–Newman solution for a rotating charged body, [[Brandon Carter]] remarked that the solutions predict a [[gyromagnetic ratio]] of 2, equal to that predicted by the relativistic quantum-mechanical [[Dirac equation]], and close to that experimentally observed for the [[electron]].<ref name=Carter-1968/>{{rp|1562}} This led to the application of the Kerr–Newman metric to create non-quantum models of the electron based on general relativity. The electron and all similar particles have large charge-to-mass ratios, which have Kerr–Newman parameters in the regime where there is no event horizon but there is a naked singularity.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Burinskii |first=Alexander |arxiv=hep-th/0507109 |title=The Dirac–Kerr–Newman electron |journal=Gravitation and Cosmology |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=109–122 |date=April 2008 |bibcode=2008GrCo...14..109B |doi=10.1134/S0202289308020011 |s2cid=119084073 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Arcos |first=H. I. |last2=Pereira |first2=J. G. |date=November 2004 |title=Kerr–Newman Solution as a Dirac Particle |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1023/B:GERG.0000046832.71368.a5 |journal=General Relativity and Gravitation |language=en |volume=36 |issue=11 |pages=2441–2464 |doi=10.1023/B:GERG.0000046832.71368.a5 |issn=0001-7701|arxiv=hep-th/0210103 }}</ref>{{rp|2442|q=The structure of the KN solution changes deeply when {{nowrap|''m''<sup>2</sup> < ''a''<sup>2</sup> + ''q''<sup>2</sup>}}. Due to the absence of an horizon, it does not represent a black hole, but a circular naked singularity in spacetime.}} For example, for the electron the charge-to-mass ratio {{nowrap|2''r''<sub>''Q''</sub> / ''r''<sub>s</sub> ≈ 10<sup>21</sup>}} and the spin effects are both orders of magnitude larger than this limit.<ref name="Kjell"/> 

If the Kerr–Newman potential is considered as a classical model for an electron it predicts an electron having not only a magnetic dipole moment, but also other multipole moments, such as an electric quadrupole moment.<ref name=Newman-2014>{{cite journal |last1=Newman |first1=Ezra (Ted) |last2=Adamo |first2=Tim |date=October 23, 2014 |title=Kerr–Newman metric |journal=Scholarpedia |language=en |volume=9 |issue=10 |article-number=31791 |doi=10.4249/scholarpedia.31791 |arxiv=1410.6626 |bibcode=2014SchpJ...931791N |doi-access=free |issn=1941-6016}}</ref> However, no experimental measurements of such a quadrupole moment have been reported.<ref name="Kjell">{{cite journal |last=Rosquist |first=Kjell |title=Gravitationally induced electromagnetism at the Compton scale |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=23 |issue=9 |pages=3111–3122 |year=2006 |arxiv=gr-qc/0412064 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/23/9/021 |bibcode=2006CQGra..23.3111R |s2cid=15285753 }}</ref>
